name: Rolling Forecasts
title: Rolling Forecasts
answer: Rolling forecasts are a planning method that keeps a fixed horizon, such as twelve or eighteen months, and adds a new period as the oldest period drops off. They cover the same core areas as an annual budget, including revenue, costs, cash flow, headcount, and capital expenditure, but they are refreshed on a monthly or quarterly cadence. The scope often includes driver-based models that connect operational metrics, such as units sold or employee turnover, to financial outcomes. They sit within forecasting and planning alongside the annual budget and the long-range plan, and they give managers a current view instead of a view that ages over the year.

The scope often includes driver-based models that connect operational metrics, such as units sold or employee turnover, to financial outcomes. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Rolling forecasts run on a mix of spreadsheets, enterprise resource planning systems, and dedicated enterprise performance management platforms. Source data comes from general ledgers, billing systems, customer relationship management tools, and operational databases, often through a cloud data warehouse or an integration layer. Planning tools hold the model structure, versions, and calculations, while business intelligence tools present the results. Where statistical or machine learning models are used, they typically run alongside the planning platform rather than replacing it, and they depend on clean master data and a reliable close process.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts with a defined cadence, usually monthly or quarterly, and a clear cut-off for actuals. The team loads actual results, updates the drivers and assumptions, and runs the model to produce a new forecast for the fixed horizon. Analysts compare the new forecast with the previous version and the budget, then investigate variances with business partners. Many teams use statistical baselines or machine learning for seasonality and trend, but they keep a driver-based model for the parts of the business that management can influence. The output is reviewed, documented, and published to decision makers.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in rolling forecasts centre on data provenance, version control, auditability, and clear ownership of assumptions and models. Each number should trace back to a source system or a documented assumption, and each change should record who made it and when. Access controls separate those who can edit drivers from those who can only view results, and model documentation explains the logic for internal and external reviewers. Forecasts are estimates, not guarantees, so they carry bias, data quality, and model risk, especially when machine learning is used. Where forecasts feed into regulated reporting or contractual covenants, the controls around them need to be as strong as those around the actuals.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Rolling forecasts are moving from a periodic exercise toward a more continuous process, with event-driven updates and tighter links to operational systems. AI and machine learning are being used for anomaly detection, probabilistic ranges, and narrative generation, while humans keep ownership of assumptions and decisions. Planning platforms are adding real-time data connectors and scenario engines, so the forecast can be re-run when a major order, supply disruption, or price change occurs. The direction is toward fewer manual reconciliations and more explainable models, because a forecast that cannot be traced or understood will not be trusted. Governance and provenance will likely grow in importance as the cadence increases.
